Question 1: LDA

Let’s start by estimating the components of LDA. From the lecture notes, for each target point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_0, we find the class label kk with the largest score

𝐱0𝖳𝚺−1𝛍k−12𝛍k𝖳𝚺−1𝛍k+logπk. \mathbf{x}_0^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_k -\frac12\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_k +\log\pi_k.

Thus, we need to estimate:

  • the prior probabilities πk\pi_k;
  • the mean vector (centroid) 𝛍k\boldsymbol{\mu}_k for each class; and
  • the pooled covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.

Use saheart.csv, the SAheart data from ElemStatLearn. The two classes are defined by chd, the coronary heart disease indicator. Use all nine other variables as numerical predictors, coding famhist as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present. The following code constructs an n×9n\times9 predictor matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} and an nn-entry response vector 𝐲\mathbf{y}, where nn is the number of observations.

  • R
  • Python
heart <- read.csv("data/saheart.csv")
heart$famhist <- factor(heart$famhist, levels = c("Absent", "Present"))
X <- data.matrix(heart[, names(heart) != "chd"])
y <- heart$chd
import pandas as pd

heart["famhist"] = heart["famhist"].map({"Absent": 1, "Present": 2})
X = heart.drop(columns="chd").to_numpy()
y = heart["chd"].to_numpy()

heart <- read.csv(

classes <- sort(unique(y))
n <- nrow(X)
K <- length(classes)

priors <- sapply(classes, function(k) mean(y == k))
names(priors) <- classes

mu <- t(sapply(classes, function(k) {
  colMeans(X[y == k, , drop = FALSE])
}))
rownames(mu) <- classes

centered <- X - mu[match(y, classes), ]

Sigma <- crossprod(centered) / (n - K)

  1. Use your estimated values to predict the label of each observation in the training data. These are in-sample fitted labels. Provide the confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. Check that the dimensions of your matrices and vectors match. Calculate the scores yourself for this part.
weights <- solve(Sigma, t(mu))

intercepts <- -0.5 * rowSums(mu * t(weights)) + log(priors)

scores <- sweep(X %*% weights, 2, intercepts, FUN = "+")
colnames(scores) <- classes

pred_manual <- classes[max.col(scores, ties.method = "first")]

list(
  X = dim(X),
  mu = dim(mu),
  Sigma = dim(Sigma),
  weights = dim(weights),
  intercepts = length(intercepts),
  scores = dim(scores),
  predictions = length(pred_manual)
)

Question 2: QDA and marginal screening

In the lecture, ordinary QDA could not be fitted to the handwritten digit sample because its within-class covariance matrices were singular. Let’s consider selecting fewer variables and see whether this helps. For this question, use the full zip-train.csv.gz as the training data and zip-test.csv.gz as the test data, with all ten digit classes. These are the original zip.train and zip.test data from ElemStatLearn. Each file has no header: the first column is the digit label and the remaining 256 columns are pixel values.

Instead of using all 256 predictors, select the 40 with the largest marginal variances in the training data. Here, marginal variance means the variance of one pixel across all training observations. Use the original pixel values without standardizing them, and retain the same selected predictors in the test data.

Use MASS::qda in R or QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(tol=1e-8) in Python.

  1. Fit QDA using these 40 predictors and report the test confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. Also report the test misclassification rate.
library(MASS)

train <- read.csv(gzfile("data/zip-train.csv.gz"), header = FALSE)
test <- read.csv(gzfile("data/zip-test.csv.gz"), header = FALSE)

X_train <- as.matrix(train[, -1])
X_test <- as.matrix(test[, -1])

y_train <- factor(train[, 1], levels = 0:9)
y_test <- factor(test[, 1], levels = 0:9)

pixel_variances <- apply(X_train, 2, var)
ranked_pixels <- order(pixel_variances, decreasing = TRUE)
selected_40 <- ranked_pixels[1:40]

X_train_40 <- X_train[, selected_40, drop = FALSE]
X_test_40 <- X_test[, selected_40, drop = FALSE]

fit_40 <- qda(x = X_train_40, grouping = y_train)

pred_40 <- predict(fit_40, newdata = X_test_40)$class

cm_40 <- table(
  Observed = y_test,
  Predicted = factor(pred_40, levels = 0:9)
)

error_40 <- mean(pred_40 != y_test)

I selected the 40 pixels with the largest marginal variances in the training data. Each variance was calculated across all training observations, without separating the digit classes. I retained the same selected pixels in the test data and used their original values without standardization.

I fitted QDA using these 40 predictors and empirical class priors. The output above shows the test confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. The test misclassification rate was 0.1555, or 15.55%.

  1. Does the method work? Why do you think it works or does not work?
ranks_40 <- sapply(levels(y_train), function(k) {
  class_data <- X_train_40[y_train == k, , drop = FALSE]
  qr(cov(class_data))$rank
})

data.frame(
  Digit = levels(y_train),
  Covariance_rank = unname(ranks_40)
)

The method works computationally because QDA can be fitted using the selected 40 predictors. The within-class covariance matrices have full rank, so they can be inverted.

Reducing the number of predictors reduces the number of covariance parameters that must be estimated for each digit class. Selecting pixels with large marginal variances also favors pixels that vary across images and removes many pixels with little variation. However, large overall variance does not necessarily mean that a pixel helps distinguish digit classes, and reducing the number of predictors does not always guarantee nonsingular within-class covariance matrices.

  1. Repeat the analysis using the 10 predictors with the largest marginal variances in the training data. How does the test misclassification rate compare with the 40-predictor version? Why do you think this happens?

The test misclassification rate was 34.23% for the 10-predictor model, compared with 15.55% for the 40-predictor model. Thus, the 10-predictor model had a higher test misclassification rate.

Using fewer predictors involves a tradeoff. With 10 predictors, QDA estimates fewer covariance parameters, which can make estimation more stable. However, it also discards pixels that may contain useful information for distinguishing digits. A higher error rate would suggest that the loss of useful information outweighs the benefit of simpler covariance estimation; a lower error rate would suggest that reducing estimation variability is beneficial.

Question 3: Compare LDA and QDA

In this simulation, we will study how the relative performance of LDA and QDA changes with the true covariance structure. The parameter ρ\rho controls the distribution from which we generate the data; it is not a tuning parameter of LDA or QDA.

Consider a classification problem with two equally likely classes, labeled 1 and 2, and p=10p=10 covariates. The first two covariates have the class-conditional distributions

(X1X2)∣Y=1∼N2((−10),(1ρρ1)), \begin{pmatrix}X_1\\X_2\end{pmatrix}\mid Y=1 \sim N_2\left( \begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix} \right),

(X1X2)∣Y=2∼N2((10),(1−ρ−ρ1)). \begin{pmatrix}X_1\\X_2\end{pmatrix}\mid Y=2 \sim N_2\left( \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}1&-\rho\\-\rho&1\end{pmatrix} \right).

In both classes, the remaining eight covariates are independent standard normal variables, independent of the first two. Consider

ρ∈{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9}. \rho\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9\}.

For each value of ρ\rho, generate 100 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations from each class. Fit ordinary LDA and QDA using all 10 covariates and equal class priors. Estimate the class means from the training data, with one pooled covariance matrix for LDA and one full covariance matrix per class for QDA. Set a random seed and report it.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of ρ\rho. Fit both methods and calculate their test misclassification rates. Within each setting, use the same training and test observations for the two methods.
library(MASS)

set.seed(432)

rho_values <- c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9)

generate_data <- function(n_per_class, rho) {

  make_class <- function(label) {
    z <- matrix(
      rnorm(n_per_class * 10),
      nrow = n_per_class,
      ncol = 10
    )

    correlation <- if (label == 1) rho else -rho

    x <- z
    x[, 1] <- z[, 1] + if (label == 1) -1 else 1
    x[, 2] <- correlation * z[, 1] +
      sqrt(1 - correlation^2) * z[, 2]

    x
  }

  list(
    X = rbind(make_class(1), make_class(2)),
    y = factor(rep(1:2, each = n_per_class))
  )
}

run_experiment <- function(rho) {
  train <- generate_data(100, rho)
  test <- generate_data(1000, rho)

  lda_fit <- lda(
    x = train$X,
    grouping = train$y,
    prior = c(0.5, 0.5)
  )

  qda_fit <- qda(
    x = train$X,
    grouping = train$y,
    prior = c(0.5, 0.5)
  )

  c(
    LDA = mean(predict(lda_fit, test$X)$class != test$y),
    QDA = mean(predict(qda_fit, test$X)$class != test$y)
  )
}

single_results <- data.frame(
  rho = rho_values,
  t(sapply(rho_values, run_experiment))
)

knitr::kable(single_results, digits = 4)

  1. At each fixed value of ρ\rho, repeat the experiment 50 times, generating new training and test observations in each repetition. Plot average test error against ρ\rho in one figure, with one curve for LDA and one for QDA. These curves compare performance across different data-generating distributions.
set.seed(433)

B <- 50

average_results <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(rho_values, function(rho) {

    errors <- replicate(B, run_experiment(rho))

    data.frame(
      rho = rho,
      LDA = mean(errors["LDA", ]),
      QDA = mean(errors["QDA", ])
    )
  })
)

I used random seed 433 for the repeated simulation. At each fixed value of rho, I repeated the experiment 50 times, generating new training and test observations in every repetition. Within each repetition, LDA and QDA used the same observations.

LDA’s average test error remained close to 17% across the settings. QDA had higher average error at small values of rho, but its error decreased substantially at large values. QDA outperformed LDA at rho = 0.8 and 0.9. These curves compare different data-generating distributions; rho is not a tuning parameter of either fitted method.

  1. Compare the two methods at small and large values of ρ\rho. How does changing the true covariance structure affect their relative performance? Explain the pattern using their covariance assumptions and the bias-variance trade-off. How can the eight noise covariates affect performance even though they contain no information about the class label?

When rho is zero, both classes have the same covariance matrix, so LDA’s shared-covariance assumption is correct. LDA pools observations from both classes to estimate one covariance matrix, giving it lower estimation variance than QDA. QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, which introduces additional variability without a population-level advantage when the covariances are equal.

At small positive values of rho, the class covariance matrices differ only modestly. LDA’s lower estimation variance can still outweigh the bias from assuming a common covariance matrix. This explains its lower average test error in these settings.

At large values of rho, the first two covariates have a strong positive correlation in class 1 and a strong negative correlation in class 2. QDA can use this difference through a quadratic decision boundary. LDA pools the two opposing correlations, which approximately cancel, and cannot fully use the class-specific covariance structure. QDA’s reduction in bias then outweighs its greater estimation variance, leading to lower average test error.

The eight noise covariates contain no information about the class label, but their estimated means, variances, and correlations fluctuate in finite samples. These random differences can influence the fitted decision boundaries and hurt test performance. This is especially relevant for QDA: with 10 predictors, it estimates 55 distinct covariance entries per class, compared with 55 total for LDA’s pooled covariance matrix.

# LDA/QDA Analysis

Apply this workflow only when explicitly invoked with a dataset, response, predictor list, and any coding or split requirements. Do not assume variable names, data properties, or results.

## Analysis

1. Validate the requested columns, outcome classes, predictor coding, missingness, and whether the requested models can be fit. Treat predictors as numeric or categorical only as directed; do not silently recode or omit observations.
2. If a holdout is requested, reserve it before model selection using the specified seed and stratification rule. Keep it out of preprocessing, cross-validation, candidate selection, and revisions. Do not evaluate it until the user authorizes the final evaluation.
3. Compare ordinary LDA and QDA. Add only LDA/QDA-based extensions explicitly requested or permitted, such as PCA followed by LDA/QDA or fixed probability blends. Use empirical class priors unless directed otherwise.
4. Compare candidates on identical stratified folds and repeats, using the requested seed and metric. Estimate every preprocessing step (including centering, scaling, and PCA) using only each fold's analysis portion; apply that fitted transform to its validation portion. Record fold-level results, warnings, and failures. Do not hide unsuccessful fits.
5. Select by the requested cross-validation metric. State any deterministic tie rule. Review the complete candidate results and revise only with training/CV evidence. Report the selected CV error as an estimate subject to selection optimism; do not present it as holdout performance.
6. Supply executable, reproducible R code with explicit seeds, candidate definitions, fold construction, preprocessing, fitting, scoring, and outputs. Keep all classifiers within LDA, QDA, or combinations of their probabilities.

## Report

Produce a clearly readable analysis report that fits on at most one printed page. Include:

- Dataset, response/predictor coding, split and validation design, and seeds.
- A figure of candidate cross-validation errors and a compact table of numerical results.
- Candidate descriptions, selected method/settings, CV misclassification estimate, and numerical fitting details such as class counts or empirical priors.

SAheart: Comparing LDA and QDA

Data and methods. The response was chd, using all nine remaining variables as numerical predictors, with famhist coded Absent = 1 and Present = 2. All 462 observations were complete. A stratified split (seed 432) assigned 346 observations to training and 116 to a reserved test set. Training class counts were 226 and 120; test class counts were 76 and 40 for classes 0 and 1, respectively.

The 19 candidates were ordinary LDA and QDA; standardized PCA with 2–8 components followed by either method; and blends of ordinary LDA/QDA probabilities with LDA weights 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75. All used empirical class priors. Candidates shared stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated five times (seed 433). Scaling and PCA were estimated separately within each fold’s training observations. Selection minimized mean cross-validation misclassification rate.

Selected model and test performance. Six-component PCA followed by LDA had the lowest cross-validation error, 26.53%. Its preprocessing and classifier were refitted on all training observations, then evaluated once on the reserved test set. There were 34 errors among 116 observations, giving a 29.31% test misclassification rate and 70.69% accuracy. The confusion matrix was:

Observed class Predicted 0 Predicted 1
0 62 14
1 20 20

Findings and limitations. The selected model improved cross-validation error over ordinary LDA by 1.45 percentage points. Dimension reduction may reduce estimation variability, while QDA requires estimating separate covariance matrices. The modest validation advantage does not establish a definitive performance difference. Limitations include the small test set, a single train/test split, model-selection uncertainty, and Gaussian and shared-covariance assumptions. Test outcomes were not used to revise the model.
